lessons.title: The Alphabet and Spelling
lessons.summary: Say the 26 letters, spell your name, and avoid the letters French speakers mix up.
lessons.explanation:
Say the letters in groups that share a sound:
/eɪ/: A H J K · /iː/: B C D E G P T V Z · /e/: F L M N S X · /aɪ/: I Y · /əʊ/: O · /uː/: Q U W · /ɑː/: R.
The big French traps: E is 'ee' and I is 'eye' (the opposite of French!); G is 'jee' and J is 'jay'; A sounds like 'ay'; R is 'ar'; W is 'double-you'.
Z is 'zed' in Canada and the UK, 'zee' in the US.
Spelling a name: 'How do you spell that?' — 'M-A-R-I-E, Marie.' Double letters: 'double L', 'double S'.
Email addresses: @ = 'at', . = 'dot', _ = 'underscore', - = 'dash' or 'hyphen'.
lessons.explanation_fr: Attention : E se dit « i » et I se dit « aï » en anglais. G = « dji », J = « djé ».

examples.en: How do you spell your surname? — L-E-M-I-E-U-X.
My email is anna dot roy at example dot com.
It's spelled with a double S.
Z is pronounced 'zed' in Canada.

exercises.prompt: Which letter is pronounced like the word 'eye'?
Which letter sounds like 'ee'?
How do you say '@' in an email address?
Which group of letters all share the same vowel sound?
In Canada, the last letter of the alphabet is usually pronounced…

lessons.title: Greetings and Introductions
lessons.summary: Hello, how are you, nice to meet you: starting and ending a conversation.
lessons.explanation:
Greetings: Hello / Hi (informal) / Good morning (until noon) / Good afternoon / Good evening. 'Good night' is only for going to bed or leaving at night.
Asking how someone is: 'How are you?' — 'I'm fine/good, thanks. And you?' Informal: 'How's it going?' — 'Not bad!'
Introducing yourself: 'My name's Paul. I'm from Lyon. I work in finance.' Meeting someone: 'Nice to meet you.' — 'Nice to meet you too.'
Introducing others: 'This is my colleague, Sarah.'
Saying goodbye: 'Bye!', 'See you later/tomorrow', 'Have a nice day!'
Note: 'How do you do?' is very formal and rare today.
lessons.explanation_fr: « Enchanté » = Nice to meet you. « Bonne nuit » ne s'utilise que pour aller se coucher.

examples.en: Hi, I'm Lucas. Nice to meet you.
This is Mei, my new colleague.
How's it going? — Pretty good, thanks!
See you tomorrow! Have a good evening.

exercises.prompt: It's 10 a.m. You meet your manager. You say:
Someone says 'Nice to meet you.' You answer:
To introduce your friend, you say:
I call myself Sophie.
exercises.explanation: « Je m'appelle » = My name is / I'm.

exercises.prompt: 'How are you?' — Choose the best answer:

lessons.title: Numbers, Dates and Time
lessons.summary: Counting, prices, phone numbers, days, months, dates and telling the time.
lessons.explanation:
Numbers: 13 thirteen vs 30 thirty (stress: thirTEEN, THIRty). 100 = a hundred, 1,000 = a thousand. English uses a comma for thousands (1,500) and a point for decimals (2.5).
Prices: $4.99 = 'four ninety-nine' or 'four dollars ninety-nine'.
Ordinals: 1st first, 2nd second, 3rd third, 4th fourth… 21st twenty-first.
Dates: 'on Monday', 'in March', 'on March 5th' / 'on the 5th of March'. Days and months take a capital letter in English. North America often writes 03/05 for March 5.
Time: 3:15 = 'quarter past three' / 'three fifteen'; 3:30 = 'half past three'; 3:45 = 'quarter to four'. a.m. (morning) / p.m. (afternoon and evening).
lessons.explanation_fr: Majuscule aux jours et mois : Monday, March. Virgule pour les milliers, point pour les décimales : 1,500.50.

examples.en: My birthday is on July 14th.
The meeting is at half past two.
It costs twenty-nine ninety-nine.
My number is five-one-four, five-five-five, oh-one-two-three.

exercises.prompt: Which is 13?
I start work ___ Monday ___ 9 a.m.
My birthday is in the 3 june.
answer: My birthday is on the 3rd of June.
exercises.explanation: on + date; capital letter for months.

exercises.prompt: The ___ month of the year is March.

lessons.title: Shopping and Services
lessons.summary: Asking for things, prices, sizes and paying in shops and restaurants.
lessons.explanation:
Asking: 'Can I have…?', 'Could I get…?', 'I'd like…' (= I would like, polite). 'Do you have this in a medium / in blue?'
Prices: 'How much is it?' (one thing) / 'How much are they?' (plural). 'That comes to $24.50.'
Paying: 'Can I pay by card?', 'Do you take cash?', 'Can I tap?' (contactless). 'Would you like a receipt / a bag?'
Restaurants: 'A table for two, please.' 'Could we have the bill/check, please?' (UK bill, North America check). Tipping in Canada and the US: usually 15–20%.
Returns: 'I'd like to return this.' 'Can I exchange it for a smaller size?'
lessons.explanation_fr: « Je voudrais » = I'd like (pas *I want, trop direct). « L'addition » = the bill (UK) / the check (Canada, US).

examples.en: I'd like a large coffee, please.
Do you have these shoes in a size 9?
Could we have the check, please?
I'd like to return this sweater. It's too small.

exercises.prompt: Choose the most polite request:
___ are these jeans?
In a Canadian restaurant you ask for:
Can I pay ___ card?
Do you have this in more small?
answer: Do you have this in a smaller size?
Do you have this in small?
Do you have this in a small?

lessons.title: Travel and Directions
lessons.summary: Airports, hotels, public transport and asking for directions.
lessons.explanation:
At the airport: 'Where do I check in?', 'Is this the gate for Calgary?', 'My flight is delayed / cancelled.' boarding pass, carry-on, checked baggage.
At the hotel: 'I have a reservation under the name Martin.' 'What time is check-out?' 'Is breakfast included?'
Transport: 'A return/round-trip ticket to Ottawa, please.' (UK return, North America round-trip). 'Which bus goes downtown?' 'Where do I get off?'
Directions: 'Excuse me, how do I get to the station?' — 'Go straight ahead, turn left at the lights, it's on your right / next to the bank / across from the park.'
'downtown' (North America) = centre-ville.
lessons.explanation_fr: « Aller-retour » = return (UK) / round-trip (North America). « En face de » = across from / opposite.

examples.en: Excuse me, how do I get to the museum?
Turn right at the corner. It's across from the church.
I have a reservation for three nights.
Our flight has been delayed by two hours.

exercises.prompt: You want to go and come back. In Canada you ask for a ___ ticket.
The bank is ___ the café. (= on the other side of the street)
At the hotel desk you say:
options: I have a reservation under the name Roy.
I have a booking on Roy.
exercises.answer: I have a reservation under the name Roy.

exercises.prompt: Go straight ___ and turn left at the lights.
Where I can take the bus for downtown?
answer: Where can I take the bus downtown?
Where can I get the bus downtown?
Where can I take the bus to downtown?
Where can I catch the bus downtown?

lessons.title: Everyday Requests, Offers and Invitations
lessons.summary: Could you…? Would you like…? Let's… How about…? Accepting and refusing politely.
lessons.explanation:
Requests: 'Can you…?' (neutral), 'Could you…?' (more polite), 'Would you mind + -ing?' (very polite): 'Could you send me the file?' 'Would you mind closing the door?'
Offers: 'Shall I…?', 'Can I help you?', 'Would you like some water?' (would like + noun / to + verb).
Invitations and suggestions: 'Would you like to come for dinner?', 'Let's meet at six.', 'How about going to the cinema?', 'Why don't we take a break?'
Accepting: 'I'd love to!', 'Sounds great!' Refusing politely: 'I'd love to, but I'm busy on Friday.', 'Thanks, but I can't make it.'
Say 'please' and 'thank you' often; direct imperatives can sound rude in English.
lessons.explanation_fr: « Ça te dirait de… ? » = How about… ? / Would you like to… ? Refuser poliment : I'd love to, but…

examples.en: Could you help me with my bags?
Would you like to join us for lunch?
How about meeting on Thursday?
I'd love to, but I've already got plans.

exercises.prompt: Would you mind ___ the window?
Your friend invites you, but you can't go. You say:
options: I'd love to, but I'm working that day.
exercises.answer: I'd love to, but I'm working that day.

exercises.prompt: How about ___ (go) for a walk?
Choose the polite offer:
options: Shall I carry that for you?
exercises.answer: Shall I carry that for you?

exercises.prompt: Would you like come to my party?
answer: Would you like to come to my party?

lessons.title: Everyday Idiomatic Expressions
lessons.summary: Common idioms that native speakers use every day, with their meaning and register.
lessons.explanation:
Idioms make your English sound natural, but use them in the right situation.
break the ice = start a conversation in a new group · a piece of cake = very easy · under the weather = slightly ill · hit the books = study hard · cost an arm and a leg = be very expensive · on the fence = undecided · call it a day = stop working for the day · get the hang of = learn how to do something · in the same boat = in the same difficult situation · once in a blue moon = very rarely.
Idioms are fixed: don't change the words ('a piece of cake', NOT *a part of cake).
lessons.explanation_fr: Les expressions idiomatiques ne se traduisent pas mot à mot : « coûter les yeux de la tête » = cost an arm and a leg.

examples.en: The exam was a piece of cake.
I'm feeling a bit under the weather today.
Let's call it a day and continue tomorrow.
Don't worry, we're all in the same boat.

exercises.prompt: 'I'm on the fence about the job offer' means:
Choose the idiom: 'The new phone was very expensive.' → It ___.
options: cost an arm and a leg
exercises.answer: cost an arm and a leg

exercises.prompt: A good joke at the start of a meeting can help ___.
It took me a week to get the ___ of the new software.
'I go to the theatre once in a blue moon' means:

lessons.title: Polite Communication at Work
lessons.summary: Softening requests, disagreeing politely, and phone and video-call phrases.
lessons.explanation:
Softening makes requests polite: 'Could you possibly…?', 'I was wondering if you could…', 'Would it be possible to…?'
Disagreeing politely: 'I see your point, but…', 'I'm not sure I agree.', 'That's a good idea; however, …'. Avoid a flat 'You're wrong.'
Asking for clarification: 'Sorry, could you repeat that?', 'What do you mean by…?', 'Just to clarify, …'
Calls: 'This is Marie from accounting.', 'Could I speak to…?', 'I'll put you through.', 'Can I leave a message?' Video calls: 'You're on mute.', 'Can everyone see my screen?', 'You're breaking up.'
Ending: 'Thanks for your time.', 'I'll get back to you by Friday.'
lessons.explanation_fr: Le conditionnel adoucit : « Pourriez-vous… » = Could you possibly… / I was wondering if you could…

examples.en: I was wondering if you could send me the slides.
I see your point, but I think we need more data.
Sorry, you're on mute.
I'll get back to you by the end of the day.

exercises.prompt: Choose the most polite request:
options: I was wondering if you could send me the report.
You must send me the report.
exercises.answer: I was wondering if you could send me the report.

exercises.prompt: In a video call, someone's sound keeps cutting out. You say:
Choose a polite way to disagree:
options: I see your point, but I'm not sure that will work.
exercises.answer: I see your point, but I'm not sure that will work.

exercises.prompt: I'll get ___ to you by Friday.
exercises.explanation: get back to someone = reply later.

exercises.prompt: Can you repeat? I didn't understand.
answer: Could you repeat that, please? I didn't understand.
Sorry, could you repeat that? I didn't understand.
Can you repeat that? I didn't understand.
exercises.explanation: repeat needs an object: repeat that.

lessons.title: Writing Structured Paragraphs
lessons.summary: Topic sentence, supporting details, linking words and a concluding sentence.
lessons.explanation:
A good paragraph develops ONE main idea.
1. Topic sentence: states the main idea. 'Working from home has several advantages.'
2. Supporting sentences: explanations, examples, details. Use linkers: firstly, also, in addition, for example, for instance, however, as a result.
3. Concluding sentence: sums up or links to the next idea. 'Overall, …', 'For these reasons, …'
Keep sentences clear: one idea per sentence; avoid very long sentences joined with commas.
Use a new paragraph for each new main idea, and leave a blank line between paragraphs in emails.
lessons.explanation_fr: Un paragraphe = une idée principale annoncée dans la première phrase.

examples.en: Topic: Public transport in my city is excellent.
For example, the metro runs every three minutes at rush hour.
In addition, tickets are cheaper than parking.
Overall, it is the best way to get around.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best topic sentence for a paragraph about exercise?
options: Regular exercise has many benefits for health.
exercises.answer: Regular exercise has many benefits for health.

exercises.prompt: Which linker introduces an example?
Which linker shows a consequence?
I like my job, it is interesting, my colleagues are nice, the salary is good.
answer: I like my job. It is interesting, my colleagues are nice and the salary is good.
I like my job because it is interesting, my colleagues are nice and the salary is good.
I like my job. It is interesting. My colleagues are nice, and the salary is good.
exercises.explanation: Avoid joining sentences with commas only.

lessons.title: Telling a Story Well
lessons.summary: Sequencing words, reacting, and keeping your listener interested.
lessons.explanation:
Structure: set the scene (when, where, who) → the problem or event → what happened next → the ending and how you felt.
Sequencing: first, at first, then, after that, later, suddenly, all of a sudden, eventually, in the end, finally.
'At the end' (= at the final point of something) ≠ 'in the end' (= finally, after a long process). 'Eventually' = finally, after a delay (NOT éventuellement).
Keep the listener engaged: 'You won't believe what happened…', 'Guess what?', 'Anyway, …'
Listeners react: 'Really?', 'No way!', 'What happened next?', 'That must have been scary!'
lessons.explanation_fr: Faux ami : « eventually » = finalement (pas « éventuellement »). « In the end » = au final.

examples.en: You won't believe what happened on my way to work.
All of a sudden, the train stopped in the tunnel.
Eventually, after an hour, we started moving again.
No way! That must have been stressful.

exercises.prompt: We waited for hours, but ___ the bus arrived.
Which phrase introduces a sudden event?
Your friend tells you a surprising story. You react:
We argued for a long time, but ___ we agreed.

lessons.title: Collocations: Words That Go Together
lessons.summary: make or do, strong or heavy, and other natural word partnerships.
lessons.explanation:
Collocations are word pairs that native speakers use together. Using the wrong partner sounds unnatural even when the meaning is clear.
make: a decision, a mistake, progress, an effort, a phone call, money, a complaint. do: homework, business, research, a favour, damage, your best.
take: a break, a photo, an exam, a risk, notes, part in. have: a meeting, a look, an argument, fun.
Adjective + noun: heavy rain/traffic, strong coffee/wind, high prices/salary, deep concern, a rough estimate, a tough decision.
Adverb + adjective: highly recommended, deeply concerned, fully aware, bitterly disappointed.
lessons.explanation_fr: « Prendre une décision » = make a decision ; « faire une erreur » = make a mistake ; « passer un examen » = take an exam.

examples.en: We need to make a decision today.
She's doing research on climate policy.
Traffic was heavy this morning.
I'm fully aware of the risks.

exercises.prompt: I ___ a mistake in the report.
There was ___ rain all night.
I'm going to ___ the IELTS exam in June.
Could you ___ me a favour?
This course is ___ recommended.

lessons.title: Debates and Presentations
lessons.summary: Presenting arguments, signposting a talk, and responding to counter-arguments.
lessons.explanation:
Signposting a presentation: 'Today I'm going to talk about…', 'First, … Then, … Finally, …', 'Let's move on to…', 'To sum up, …'.
Giving opinions: 'In my view, …', 'I'm convinced that…', 'It seems to me that…'.
Supporting arguments: 'This is supported by…', 'A clear example of this is…', 'The evidence suggests…'.
Conceding: 'Admittedly, …', 'It's true that…, but…'. Counter-arguing: 'Having said that, …', 'On the other hand, …', 'That argument overlooks…'.
Interrupting politely: 'Sorry to interrupt, but…', 'If I could just come in here…'.
lessons.explanation_fr: Pour concéder : « Certes… mais » = Admittedly…, but / It's true that…, but.

examples.en: Today I'm going to talk about the future of remote work.
Let's move on to the costs.
Admittedly, the plan is expensive, but it will save money long term.
That argument overlooks the impact on small businesses.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase moves to the next point of a presentation?
Which phrase concedes a point?
To interrupt politely you say:
options: If I could just come in here…
exercises.answer: If I could just come in here…

exercises.prompt: To sum ___, there are three main reasons.

lessons.title: Advanced Idiomatic Expressions
lessons.summary: Idioms for nuance: hedging, criticism, agreement and risk.
lessons.explanation:
At C1, idioms help you express nuance precisely.
be a far cry from = very different from (worse) · a double-edged sword = has advantages and disadvantages · beat around the bush = avoid saying something directly · the elephant in the room = an obvious problem nobody mentions · cut corners = do something badly to save money/time · play devil's advocate = argue the opposite to test an idea · a blessing in disguise = something bad that turns out good · go back to the drawing board = start planning again · (it's) not rocket science = it isn't complicated · read between the lines = understand the hidden meaning.
Register matters: most idioms are informal or neutral; avoid them in formal academic writing.
lessons.explanation_fr: Registre : évitez les idiomes dans un essai académique, utilisez-les à l'oral et dans les e-mails moins formels.

examples.en: Let me play devil's advocate for a moment.
Losing that contract was a blessing in disguise.
Nobody mentioned the budget, the elephant in the room.
The final product was a far cry from the prototype.

exercises.prompt: 'Stop beating around the bush' means:
The plan failed, so we had to go back to the ___.
'The new rules are a double-edged sword' means they…
You don't need a degree to do this; it's not rocket ___.

lessons.title: Professional Presentations
lessons.summary: Opening strongly, handling data, rhetorical techniques and Q&A.
lessons.explanation:
Strong openings: a striking figure ('Every day, we lose 40 customers.'), a question, or a short story — not 'Today I will talk about…'.
Describing data: rose sharply / steadily / slightly; fell, dropped, plummeted; levelled off; peaked at; a twofold increase; accounted for 30%.
Rhetorical techniques: the rule of three ('faster, cheaper and safer'), contrast ('not a cost, but an investment'), rhetorical questions.
Handling Q&A: 'That's a great question.', 'If I understand you correctly, you're asking…', 'I don't have that figure to hand, but I'll get back to you.'
Closing: 'Let me leave you with one thought…', 'The key takeaway is…'.
lessons.explanation_fr: Décrire une évolution : « a fortement augmenté » = rose sharply ; « s'est stabilisé » = levelled off.

examples.en: Sales rose sharply in Q3 before levelling off in Q4.
This is not a cost; it's an investment.
I don't have that figure to hand, but I'll follow up.
The key takeaway is simple: act early.

exercises.prompt: Prices increased very quickly. They ___.
After growing, sales stayed stable. They ___.
The strongest opening is usually…
options: 'Today I will talk about my slides.'

exercises.prompt: I don't have that figure to ___, but I'll send it to you.

lessons.title: Negotiating Effectively
lessons.summary: Making proposals, bargaining, conditional offers and reaching agreement.
lessons.explanation:
Opening: 'We'd like to propose…', 'Our starting point is…'.
Probing: 'What flexibility do you have on…?', 'What would it take for you to…?'
Conditional offers (the key negotiating structure): 'If you can increase the volume, we could reduce the price.' 'We'd be willing to…, provided that / as long as…'.
Refusing firmly but politely: 'I'm afraid that's not something we can agree to.', 'That's outside our budget.'
Seeking agreement: 'Shall we meet halfway?', 'I think we have a deal.', 'Let's summarise what we've agreed.'
lessons.explanation_fr: Structure clé : If you…, we could… / provided that… (à condition que).

examples.en: If you sign a two-year contract, we could offer a 10% discount.
We'd be willing to pay upfront, provided that delivery is guaranteed.
I'm afraid that's not something we can accept.
Shall we meet halfway on the price?

exercises.prompt: If you ___ the order, we could reduce the price.
We accept, ___ payment is made within 30 days.
To suggest a compromise you say:
If you will pay in advance, we can give a discount.
answer: If you pay in advance, we can give a discount.
If you pay in advance, we could give a discount.

lessons.title: Rhetoric and Persuasive Devices
lessons.summary: Antithesis, tricolon, anaphora, litotes and understatement in speech and writing.
lessons.explanation:
Antithesis: contrasting ideas in balanced phrases: 'Not because it is easy, but because it is hard.'
Tricolon: a series of three for rhythm and emphasis: 'clear, concise and compelling'.
Anaphora: repeating the opening words of successive clauses: 'We will listen. We will learn. We will act.'
Litotes: affirming by denying the opposite: 'not without merit' (= quite good), 'no small achievement' (= a great achievement).
Understatement, very British: 'It was a bit of a setback' (= a disaster).
Rhetorical questions invite agreement: 'Who would choose failure?'
Overuse sounds manipulative: one or two devices per speech is plenty.
lessons.explanation_fr: La litote existe aussi en français : « Ce n'est pas mal » = c'est bien. En anglais : not without merit, no small feat.

examples.en: This is no small achievement.
Ask not what we can afford, but what we cannot afford to lose.
The plan is simple, affordable and effective.
The results were, shall we say, a little disappointing.

exercises.prompt: 'Her proposal was not without merit' means it was…
'We came, we saw, we conquered' mainly uses…
Which sentence is antithesis?
options: It is not a cost but an investment.
exercises.answer: It is not a cost but an investment.

exercises.prompt: A British manager calls a major crisis 'a bit of a hiccup'. This is…

lessons.title: Subtle Differences in Meaning
lessons.summary: Near-synonyms that native speakers distinguish: imply/infer, economic/economical, and more.
lessons.explanation:
imply (the speaker suggests) vs infer (the listener concludes): 'Are you implying I'm wrong?' / 'I infer from your email that…'.
economic (about the economy) vs economical (saving money): 'economic growth' / 'an economical car'.
continual (repeated, with breaks) vs continuous (without interruption).
disinterested (impartial) vs uninterested (not interested).
complement (complete, go well with) vs compliment (praise).
principal (main; head of school) vs principle (a rule, belief).
flout (openly disobey) vs flaunt (show off).
fewer (countable) vs less (uncountable): 'fewer errors', 'less time'.
A C2 speaker chooses the exact word: precision is part of proficiency.
lessons.explanation_fr: Infer = déduire ; imply = sous-entendre. Economic = économique (de l'économie) ; economical = qui fait des économies.

examples.en: What can we infer from these results?
We need a disinterested judge.
The wine complements the meal perfectly.
He flouted the rules and then flaunted his bonus.

exercises.prompt: From her tone, I ___ that she was unhappy.
This car is very ___: it uses little fuel.
A judge must be ___.
The company ___ environmental regulations for years.
She paid me a lovely ___.

business.title: Clear Business Communication
business.summary: Being clear, concise and polite in everyday workplace exchanges.
business.explanation:
Lead with the point: state the purpose first ('I'm writing to confirm…', 'Quick question about…').
Be concise: one idea per sentence; cut fillers like 'I just wanted to maybe ask…'.
Polite but direct: 'Could you…by Thursday?' is better than a vague 'when you have time'.
Check understanding: 'Does that work for you?', 'Let me know if anything is unclear.'
Tone words: 'please', 'thanks', 'appreciate' soften without weakening the message.
business.explanation_fr: En anglais professionnel, on annonce l'objectif dès la première phrase.

examples.en: Quick question: is the client call still at 2 p.m.?
Could you send me the figures by Thursday?
I appreciate your help on this.

exercises.prompt: Which opening is clearest?
options: I hope you are well and everything is good and I wanted to maybe ask something.
I'm writing to confirm tomorrow's meeting time.
exercises.answer: I'm writing to confirm tomorrow's meeting time.

exercises.prompt: Which request includes a clear deadline?
options: Could you send it by Friday noon?
exercises.answer: Could you send it by Friday noon?

exercises.prompt: Let me know ___ anything is unclear.
'I appreciate your help' is…

business.title: Running and Taking Part in Meetings
business.summary: Opening, managing the agenda, interrupting, and closing with actions.
business.explanation:
Opening: 'Let's get started.', 'The purpose of today's meeting is…', 'We have three items on the agenda.'
Managing: 'Let's move on to item two.', 'We're running short of time.', 'Let's park that for now.' (postpone)
Participating: 'Can I just come in here?', 'Building on what Sam said…', 'I'd like to add something.'
Closing: 'To sum up, we've agreed…', 'Action items: Priya will… by Friday.', 'Let's schedule a follow-up.'
business.explanation_fr: « Mettons ce point de côté » = Let's park that for now.

examples.en: The purpose of today's meeting is to agree on the budget.
Let's park that and come back to it next week.
Action item: Daniel will send the revised figures by Friday.

exercises.prompt: To postpone a topic, the chair says:
To add to a colleague's idea:
Let's move ___ to item three.
A list of who does what after a meeting is called…

business.title: Business Negotiation
business.summary: Anchoring, trading concessions, conditional offers and closing a deal.
business.explanation:
Anchor: 'Our price for this volume is $120 per unit.'
Trade, don't give: 'If you commit to 12 months, we can bring the price down to $110.'
Probe interests: 'What's most important to you: price, timing or flexibility?'
Hold firm: 'That's our best offer at this stage.', 'We'd need something in return.'
Close: 'So, to confirm: $110 per unit, 12-month term, delivery in March. Do we have a deal?' Then follow up in writing.
business.explanation_fr: Ne jamais concéder sans contrepartie : If you…, we can…

examples.en: If you commit to a longer term, we can improve the price.
We'd need something in return.
To confirm, we've agreed on $110 per unit.

exercises.prompt: Which is a conditional trade?
options: If you order 500 units, we can offer 8% off.
exercises.answer: If you order 500 units, we can offer 8% off.

exercises.prompt: To ask the other side about priorities:
options: What matters most to you: price or delivery time?
exercises.answer: What matters most to you: price or delivery time?

exercises.prompt: That's our best ___ at this stage.
After agreement, you should…

business.title: Corporate Presentations
business.summary: Structuring a business presentation, presenting results and recommending action.
business.explanation:
Structure: hook → objective → 3 key points → recommendation → next steps.
Results: 'Revenue grew by 8% year on year.', 'Margins came under pressure.', 'We outperformed the market.'
Recommendation: 'We recommend that we expand into Alberta.', 'Our proposal is to…'
Visuals: 'As you can see on this slide…', 'The chart shows…', 'Let me draw your attention to…'
Close with a clear ask: 'We're asking for approval of a $2M budget.'
business.explanation_fr: Recommander : We recommend that we expand… (subjonctif : base verbale).

examples.en: Revenue grew by 8% year on year.
As you can see on this slide, costs fell in Q3.
We're asking for approval of the budget today.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase draws attention to a visual?
options: As you can see on this slide…
exercises.answer: As you can see on this slide…

exercises.prompt: Revenue went from 100 to 108 compared with last year. Revenue grew by 8% ___.
We recommend that the company ___ (open) a new office.
A strong presentation ends with…
options: a clear request or next step
exercises.answer: a clear request or next step

business.title: Business Writing Essentials
business.summary: Plain English, active voice, structure and tone in reports, memos and messages.
business.explanation:
Plain English: prefer short words ('use' not 'utilise', 'start' not 'commence', 'help' not 'facilitate').
Active voice is clearer: 'The team completed the audit' rather than 'The audit was completed by the team' (use the passive when the doer is unimportant).
Structure with headings and bullet points; put the conclusion or request first (bottom line up front).
Tone: professional, positive, not emotional. Replace 'You failed to…' with 'It seems the file wasn't attached.'
Proofread names, numbers and dates.
business.explanation_fr: Simplicité : use (pas utilise), start (pas commence). Conclusion d'abord.

examples.en: We will start the project in May.
The team completed the audit on time.
It looks like the attachment is missing.

exercises.prompt: Choose the plainer version:
options: We will commence utilisation of the tool.
We will start using the tool.
exercises.answer: We will start using the tool.

exercises.prompt: Choose the most diplomatic sentence:
options: It seems the attachment wasn't included.
exercises.answer: It seems the attachment wasn't included.

exercises.prompt: The decision was made by the board to postpone the launch.
answer: The board decided to postpone the launch.

exercises.prompt: 'Bottom line up front' means…

business.title: Professional Emails
business.summary: Subject lines, openings, requests, follow-ups and closings.
business.explanation:
Subject line: specific ('Q3 budget: approval needed by Friday').
Openings: 'Hi Sarah,' (neutral), 'Dear Mr. Roy,' (formal). 'I hope you're well' is optional.
Purpose: 'I'm writing to…', 'Following our call, …', 'As discussed, …'.
Attachments: 'Please find attached…' (formal) / 'I've attached…' (neutral).
Follow-up: 'Just following up on my email from Monday.'
Closings: 'Best regards,' 'Kind regards,' 'Thanks,' — avoid 'Cordially' (a French calque of 'Cordialement').
business.explanation_fr: « Cordialement » = Best regards / Kind regards (pas *Cordially). « Ci-joint » = Please find attached / I've attached.

examples.en: Subject: Contract renewal – signature needed by June 3
Following our call, I've attached the updated proposal.
Just following up on my email from Monday.

exercises.prompt: The best closing for a professional email is…
Which subject line is best?
Please find ___ the signed contract.
I write you for to ask a question.
answer: I'm writing to ask a question.
I am writing to ask a question.
I'm writing to you to ask a question.

business.title: Leadership and Management Language
business.summary: Giving feedback, delegating, motivating and setting expectations.
business.explanation:
Feedback (situation–behaviour–impact): 'In yesterday's meeting (S), you interrupted the client twice (B), which made it hard to finish the demo (I).'
Praise specifically: 'Your analysis of the churn data was excellent: it changed our decision.'
Delegating: 'I'd like you to take ownership of…', 'You have full authority to…', 'Let's check in on Thursday.'
Expectations: 'What I need from you is…', 'Success looks like…'.
Coaching questions: 'What options do you see?', 'What support do you need?'
business.explanation_fr: Feedback structuré : situation, comportement, impact. « Prendre en charge » = take ownership of.

examples.en: I'd like you to take ownership of the client onboarding.
Your analysis changed our decision; great work.
What support do you need from me?

exercises.prompt: Which feedback is most specific and useful?
options: In today's call, you summarised the client's needs clearly, which helped close the deal.
exercises.answer: In today's call, you summarised the client's needs clearly, which helped close the deal.

exercises.prompt: I'd like you to take ___ of the project.
A coaching question is…
'Success looks like…' is used to…

business.title: Human Resources
business.summary: Hiring, onboarding, performance reviews and workplace policies.
business.explanation:
Hiring: job posting, shortlist candidates, screen, interview, make an offer, onboard.
Contracts: full-time, part-time, permanent, fixed-term, probation period, notice period, benefits (health insurance, pension, paid time off).
Performance: performance review, objectives/KPIs, meet/exceed expectations, development plan, promotion, raise.
Leaving: resign, hand in your notice, be laid off (redundancy, not your fault), be dismissed/fired (for a reason).
Policies: code of conduct, harassment policy, remote-work policy, diversity and inclusion.
business.explanation_fr: « Licencié économique » = laid off ; « démissionner » = resign / hand in your notice ; « période d'essai » = probation period.

examples.en: We've shortlisted five candidates for the analyst role.
She handed in her notice last week.
Fifty employees were laid off after the merger.

exercises.prompt: Losing your job because the company is cutting costs is being…
The first months of a new job, when either side can end it easily, are the…
He handed in his ___ and leaves at the end of the month.
Health insurance and paid vacation are…

business.title: Marketing and Sales
business.summary: Value propositions, the sales conversation, handling objections and closing.
business.explanation:
Marketing terms: target market, customer persona, brand awareness, value proposition, conversion rate, churn, return on investment (ROI), campaign, lead.
Sales conversation: open with questions ('What challenges are you facing with…?'), listen, then link features to benefits ('…which means you save two hours a week').
Objections: 'I understand your concern about price. Many clients felt the same until they saw the time savings.'
Closing: 'Shall we set up a trial for next week?', 'What would you need to move forward?'

examples.en: Our value proposition is simple: faster reporting at half the cost.
It integrates with your CRM, which means no double data entry.
What would you need to move forward?

exercises.prompt: The percentage of visitors who buy is the…
Customers who stop using a service create…
Best response to a price objection:
options: I understand. Let me show you the savings it creates.
exercises.answer: I understand. Let me show you the savings it creates.

exercises.prompt: It's fully automated, ___ means your team saves time.

business.title: Corporate Finance
business.summary: Capital structure, valuation, budgeting and investment decisions.
business.explanation:
Key concepts: revenue, operating costs, EBITDA, net income, cash flow, working capital, capital expenditure (capex), debt vs equity financing, cost of capital, return on investment.
Investment appraisal: net present value (NPV), internal rate of return (IRR), payback period: 'The project has a positive NPV at an 8% discount rate.'
Budgeting: 'We're over/under budget', 'a variance of 5%', 'forecast vs actual'.
Capital structure: 'The company raised $50M through a bond issue.' 'Equity dilution is a concern.'
business.explanation_fr: Capex = investissements ; working capital = fonds de roulement ; equity = capitaux propres.

examples.en: The project has a positive NPV, so we should proceed.
We're 5% over budget on capex this quarter.
They financed the acquisition with debt rather than equity.

exercises.prompt: Money spent on long-term assets such as machinery is…
A project should usually be accepted if its NPV is…
Issuing new shares can lead to…
Actual costs were higher than planned: we are ___ budget.

business.title: Banking and Investment
business.summary: Accounts, loans, interest, portfolios and talking to clients about risk.
business.explanation:
Banking: chequing/savings account, overdraft, line of credit, mortgage, interest rate (fixed/variable), collateral, credit score.
Investing: portfolio, asset allocation, diversification, stocks/shares, bonds, ETFs, mutual funds, dividend, yield, risk tolerance, time horizon.
Client conversation: 'What's your investment time horizon?', 'How would you feel if your portfolio fell 15% in a year?', 'Past performance is not a guarantee of future returns.'
Canadian context: TFSA (tax-free savings account), RRSP (registered retirement savings plan).
business.explanation_fr: « Taux variable » = variable rate ; « tolérance au risque » = risk tolerance. CELI = TFSA, REER = RRSP.

examples.en: We recommend a diversified portfolio of stocks and bonds.
What's your time horizon for this money?
Your mortgage has a five-year fixed rate.

exercises.prompt: Spreading investments to reduce risk is…
An asset pledged to secure a loan is…
In Canada, the tax-free savings account is called a…
Past performance is not a ___ of future returns.

business.title: Financial Markets
business.summary: Market movements, monetary policy, and reading market commentary.
business.explanation:
Movements: stocks rallied / slumped / edged higher / were flat; the index hit a record high; volatility spiked; investors priced in a rate cut.
Players: central bank, institutional investors, hedge funds, retail investors, market makers.
Monetary policy: 'The central bank held rates steady.', 'hawkish' (favouring higher rates) vs 'dovish' (favouring lower rates), 'quantitative tightening'.
Instruments: equities, fixed income, derivatives (futures, options), currencies (FX), commodities.
Commentary style: 'Shares fell 4% after the company cut its guidance.'
business.explanation_fr: Hawkish = favorable à des taux plus élevés ; dovish = favorable à des baisses de taux.

examples.en: Markets rallied after the central bank signalled a rate cut.
The governor's tone was more hawkish than expected.
Shares slumped 6% after the profit warning.

exercises.prompt: A central banker who favours higher interest rates is…
'Stocks edged higher' means they…
Futures and options are…
Investors have already ___ in a rate cut, so the announcement had little effect.

business.title: Economics for Professionals
business.summary: Inflation, growth, employment and policy: discussing the economy confidently.
business.explanation:
Indicators: GDP growth, inflation (CPI), unemployment rate, interest rates, exchange rate, trade balance, consumer confidence.
Cycle: expansion, peak, slowdown, recession, recovery. 'The economy contracted for two consecutive quarters.'
Policy: monetary policy (central bank: interest rates) vs fiscal policy (government: taxes and spending). Stimulus vs austerity.
Cause and effect: 'Higher rates tend to cool demand.', 'A weaker dollar boosts exports.'
Hedge forecasts: 'Growth is expected to slow to around 1%.'
business.explanation_fr: Politique monétaire (banque centrale) ≠ politique budgétaire (fiscal policy, gouvernement).

examples.en: Inflation eased to 2.4% in October.
A weaker dollar tends to boost exports.
Growth is expected to slow next year.

exercises.prompt: Government decisions on taxes and spending are…
Two consecutive quarters of falling GDP is commonly called a…
Higher interest rates tend to ___ demand.
Inflation is ___ to fall to 2% next year. (hedged forecast)

business.title: Project Management
business.summary: Scope, milestones, risks, status updates and stakeholder communication.
business.explanation:
Lifecycle: initiation, planning, execution, monitoring, closure. Scope, deliverables, milestones, dependencies, critical path, resources.
Status updates (RAG: red/amber/green): 'We're on track for the March milestone.', 'We're two weeks behind schedule because of a vendor delay.'
Risks: 'The main risk is…; to mitigate it, we will…'. Issues = risks that have happened.
Change: 'This is a change in scope; it will affect the timeline and budget.' Avoid scope creep.
Stakeholders: sponsor, steering committee, project team, end users.
business.explanation_fr: « Dans les temps » = on track / on schedule ; « en retard » = behind schedule.

examples.en: We're on track to deliver the first milestone in March.
The main risk is supplier delay; we've identified a backup vendor.
That request is a change in scope.

exercises.prompt: A project that is progressing as planned is…
Uncontrolled growth of project requirements is…
A risk that has actually happened becomes…
We are two weeks ___ schedule.

business.title: Business Job Interviews
business.summary: Answering competency questions with STAR, talking about strengths and asking good questions.
business.explanation:
Common questions: 'Tell me about yourself.', 'Why do you want this role?', 'Tell me about a time you handled a conflict.', 'What's your greatest weakness?'
STAR method: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Use 'I' for your actions and quantify results ('…which reduced errors by 30%').
Strengths with evidence: 'I'm analytical: in my last role I built a model that…'
Weakness: genuine but improving: 'I used to find delegating hard, so I…'
Your questions: 'What does success look like in the first six months?', 'How is the team structured?'
business.explanation_fr: Méthode STAR : situation, tâche, action, résultat (chiffré si possible).

examples.en: In my last role, I led a team of four analysts.
As a result, processing time dropped by 30%.
What does success look like in the first six months?

exercises.prompt: In STAR, the 'R' stands for…
The best answer quantifies the result, for example:
options: We reduced costs by 15% in six months.
It was a success, I think.
exercises.answer: We reduced costs by 15% in six months.

exercises.prompt: A good question to ask the interviewer:
options: How much vacation do I get on day one?
What does success look like in this role?
exercises.answer: What does success look like in this role?

exercises.prompt: Tell me about a ___ when you had to manage a conflict.

business.title: Professional Networking
business.summary: Introducing yourself, small talk, the elevator pitch and following up.
business.explanation:
Opening: 'Hi, I don't think we've met. I'm Ana, I work in risk at…', 'Is this your first time at this conference?'
Elevator pitch (30 seconds): who you are, what you do, what problem you solve, what you're looking for.
Small talk topics: the event, the speakers, travel, industry news. Avoid: salary, politics, religion.
Keeping it going: open questions ('What brings you here?', 'How did you get into fintech?').
Exiting politely: 'It was great talking to you. Let's connect on LinkedIn.' Follow up within 48 hours.
business.explanation_fr: Pitch en 30 secondes : qui vous êtes, ce que vous faites, ce que vous cherchez.

examples.en: Hi, I don't think we've met. I'm Paul, I work in data analytics.
What brought you to the conference?
It was great talking to you. Let's stay in touch.

exercises.prompt: The best way to start a conversation with a stranger at an event:
options: Hi, I don't think we've met. I'm…
exercises.answer: Hi, I don't think we've met. I'm…

exercises.prompt: A 30-second summary of who you are and what you do is…
Which topic should you avoid in networking small talk?
It was great talking to you. Let's stay in ___.

business.title: Executive Communication
business.summary: Speaking to senior leaders: brevity, the bottom line, and handling tough questions.
business.explanation:
Executives want the conclusion first: 'Bottom line: we need $2M more to launch on time.'
Use the pyramid principle: answer → 3 supporting reasons → details only if asked.
Be decisive but honest: 'My recommendation is…', 'The trade-off is…', 'The main risk is…'.
Numbers over adjectives: 'a 12% drop' not 'a big drop'.
Tough questions: 'That's a fair challenge.', 'Here's what we know and what we don't.', 'I'll come back to you with the figure by end of day.'
business.explanation_fr: Le « bottom line » d'abord, puis trois raisons.

examples.en: Bottom line: we recommend delaying the launch by one month.
The trade-off is a short delay versus a much lower risk of failure.
Here's what we know, and what we don't yet know.

exercises.prompt: When briefing a CEO, start with…
Which is more executive-ready?
options: Sales dropped 12% in Q3, mainly in Ontario.
exercises.answer: Sales dropped 12% in Q3, mainly in Ontario.

exercises.prompt: My ___ is that we pause the project until Q2.
If you don't know a figure, say:
options: I'll come back to you with it by end of day.
exercises.answer: I'll come back to you with it by end of day.

business.title: Business Reports and Analysis
business.summary: Executive summaries, describing findings, cautious conclusions and recommendations.
business.explanation:
Structure: executive summary → background → findings → analysis → conclusions → recommendations → appendices.
Executive summary: half a page; the decision-maker should understand everything from it alone.
Describing findings: 'The data indicate that…', 'Customer churn increased markedly among users aged 18–24.'
Cautious analysis: 'This suggests…', 'appears to be driven by…', 'is likely to…'.
Recommendations: numbered, actionable, with owner and timeline: '1. Launch a retention campaign targeting new users (Marketing, Q2).'
business.explanation_fr: Constats : The data indicate that… ; prudence : This suggests…

examples.en: The data indicate a strong link between onboarding time and churn.
This appears to be driven by slower delivery times.
1. Reduce onboarding to under 7 days (Operations, by Q3).

exercises.prompt: The section a busy executive reads first is the…
Which phrasing is appropriately cautious?
options: This proves that price is the only factor.
This suggests that price is a major factor.
exercises.answer: This suggests that price is a major factor.

exercises.prompt: A good recommendation includes…
options: an action, an owner and a timeline
exercises.answer: an action, an owner and a timeline

exercises.prompt: The data ___ that churn is highest among new users. (formal: show)
